questions.learningObjective: Explain why product-to-sum rewrites expose beat frequencies
questions.stem: Describe how to turn a product of cosines into a sum, and explain why astronomers use it for beat patterns.

answer.exemplar: The product-to-sum identity 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A - B) converts a product into two cosines. Beat patterns arise because two close frequencies produce a slow cosine whose argument is the difference A - B, so beating happens at the difference frequency. Reducing products to sums therefore exposes the beat term directly.

questions.explanation: With 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A - B), the difference frequency appears as one of the summed terms. That slow term is exactly what an observer hears or sees as a beat.
questions.hint: Write the product as cos of the sum plus cos of the difference.

answer.exemplar: Since the sine of 180 minus x equals the sine of x, the sum is 2 sin x. The two arguments of the sine sum to 180 degrees, so the half-sum is always 90 degrees.

questions.explanation: When two sine arguments add to 180 degrees their half-sum is 90 degrees, and the sine of 90 degrees is one. The identity then leaves a single factor that reproduces the constant sum.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why inverse functions have different principal ranges
questions.stem: Explain why the inverse sine and the inverse tangent functions have different principal ranges.

answer.exemplar: The inverse sine function is the inverse of sine restricted to the interval from minus 90 to 90 degrees, because that is where sine is strictly increasing. Tangent is strictly increasing on the open interval from minus 90 to 90 degrees, so the inverse tangent shares those bounds. The ranges differ only at the endpoints, which is why arcsin can reach 90 degrees while arctan approaches but never attains it.

questions.explanation: Each inverse is built by restricting the original function to a one-to-one interval, and the range of the inverse is that interval. Sine is one-to-one on the closed interval and tangent on the open one, so their ranges differ at the endpoints.
questions.hint: The range of an inverse is where the original is one-to-one.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how product-to-sum reveals hidden frequencies
questions.stem: Explain how product-to-sum identities reveal the sum and difference frequencies hidden inside a product.

answer.exemplar: A product such as 2 cos A cos B hides two frequencies, the sum A plus B and the difference A minus B. Rewriting it as cos of the sum plus cos of the difference makes both frequencies visible as separate terms. Observers measuring stellar oscillations or radio interference use this to read off the beat frequency, which is the difference term.

questions.explanation: The product-to-sum identities turn one product into a sum of two terms whose arguments are the sum and the difference of the original angles. Those arguments are exactly the two frequencies present in the signal.
questions.hint: Ask which two angles appear after the rewrite.
